query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin nickel layer before consolidation in a tungsten–copper composite will reduce interfacial thermal resistance and improve overall thermal conductivity, while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional W–Cu composites produced by powder consolidation without any interfacial modification between tungsten and copper phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform, controlled nickel coating (~10–20 nm thick) on tungsten particles prior to composite processing.
generation.conditions: Operating under heat‐dissipation and fusion-reactor joint conditions where high heat flux, moderate operating temperatures, and irradiation stresses are expected.
generation.structural_mediator: A graded interfacial region with a nickel interlayer that bonds the tungsten and copper phases more effectively.
generation.mechanism: The nickel layer provides an intermediate lattice and electronic structure between refractory tungsten and high-conductivity copper, thereby reducing the interfacial thermal barrier and facilitating electron transport across the interface. This should enhance the effective thermal conductivity without adversely affecting the mechanical integrity or irradiation tolerance of the composite.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an otherwise comparable, unmodified W–Cu composite, the nickel-coated composite should exhibit a measurable increase in effective thermal conductivity (roughly on the order of 10–20% improvement) while maintaining similar mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Properties of conventional W–Cu composites that have no interfacial modification.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected only if the nickel coating is optimized in thickness (around 10–20 nm) and uniformity; if the coating is too thick or nonuniform, detrimental intermetallic phases could form which might impair mechanical properties or radiation stability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of thermal conductivity improvement and long-term irradiation stability is uncertain and may vary with coating process parameters and post-processing heat treatments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten–copper composites: one with tungsten particles pre-coated with an optimized nickel layer (10–20 nm) and one control set without coating. Process both identically by powder consolidation under the same conditions. Subject the samples to thermal conductivity measurements, mechanical durability tests (e.g., flexural or tensile tests), and simulated irradiation exposure to evaluate performance under fusion-reactor relevant conditions.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Irradiation resistance (e.g., dose-dependent microstructural changes, hardness tests post exposure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nickel-coated composite fails to show at least a 10% improvement in effective thermal conductivity without compromising its mechanical or irradiation performance compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
